title: The Reed Hut at Basra: the Five Circles, the Marks on the Script, and the First Dictionary
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Azd, the Dam, and the Two Shores

stops.name: Ma'rib, the dam breaks and the Azd scatter
stops.date_confidence: tribal genealogy rather than itinerary; the dam's collapse is itself a contested tradition, not an archaeologically fixed event, and the date is conventional
stops.campa: Before there is a Basra there is a wall of stone across a wadi in Yemen, and behind it the gardens of Ma'rib. The tradition says the wall fails and the tribes of the Azd go out along the roads, some east into Oman, some north to the marshes where two rivers meet the sea. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad will be born generations into that dispersal, an Azdi among Azdis, and the men who write his life begin here because a man's tongue is held to come to him with his lineage.
suggested_refs: The Ma'rib dam and the Azd migration tradition in the Arabic genealogical literature
sources: Standard Azd tribal genealogy as repeated in Arabic biographical dictionaries (Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan)

stops.name: Interior Oman, the birth the European books give him
stops.date_confidence: year attested by consensus (100 AH); place disputed. English-language reference works give Oman, and English Wikipedia carries its own Oman sentence with a verification flag. No source names a town, and this pin marks the historic interior heartland, not a birthsite
stops.campa: Oman is Azd country, and Ibadi country, and the reference books written in Europe put his cradle here: born in the year 100 of the Hijra, carried north to Basra as a child. No town is named in any of them. The point is the interior, the palm villages under the mountain, a homeland that will claim him again twelve centuries later by putting his name over its schoolhouse doors. The Arabic biographers do not tell the story this way at all, and nobody has ever reconciled the two accounts.
suggested_refs: Encyclopaedia Britannica, entry on al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, giving Oman as birthplace

stops.name: Basra, the birth the Arabic books give him
stops.date_confidence: the Arabic-language tradition states Basra flatly and relegates Oman to 'some sources say he moved there as a child'; the contradiction with the European tradition stands open and is not resolved
stops.campa: The old city sits fifteen kilometres back from the water, a garrison town of the conquest grown into the sharpest school of Arabic in the world. Here, the Arabic tabaqat say, a poor Azdi household of Omani descent has a son in the year 100. His father is called Ahmad, and the tradition makes a small marvel of it: among the first men after the Prophet's own time to carry that name. The child will leave this city for nothing but pilgrimage, and everything Arabic grammar becomes is decided within a few streets of it.
suggested_refs: The site of Old Basra beside modern az-Zubayr, marked by the Imam Ali Mosque

stops.name: Basra, the young lion in the name
stops.date_confidence: genealogical tradition; the eponym Furhud is reported by the biographical dictionaries and cannot be checked against any document
stops.campa: He is al-Farahidi because an ancestor was called Furhud, which is to say a young lion. The nisba is the whole family archive: no estate, no office, no chain of scholars behind him, only a tribe and a beast in the name. Later, when governors send him money, this is the pedigree he stands on and does not trade. The dictionaries repeat the etymology with nothing behind it, as they repeat most things, and it survives because his students thought it worth repeating.
suggested_refs: The Farahid clan of the Azd in the classical genealogical tradition

stops.name: Basra, the congregational mosque and its rings
stops.date_confidence: inferred from documented Basran teaching practice; no source dates a session or names the mosque for every class
stops.campa: The Great Mosque, founded in the year 14 of the Hijra, is where Basra keeps its learning: rings on the floor by pillar and by subject, hadith here, poetry there, and men brought in from the desert to be asked what a word means. Kufa argues with Basra over every case ending in the language, and Basra answers with the harder method. A boy of fifteen in a reed-worker's clothes sits down in one of these rings and does not get up out of it again for fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Basra (Masjid al-Basra al-Jami'), founded 14 AH / 636 CE
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica on Basra as an early centre of Arabic scholarship
Standard tabaqat accounts of Basran teaching circles

stops.name: Basra, the circle of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'
stops.date_confidence: attested as his principal teacher in philology; no dates are given for the period of study
stops.campa: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' is one of the seven readers whose recitation of the Qur'an the whole community will follow, and the leading philologist of the city. He is the teacher the sources name first. What passes between them is method rather than doctrine: that the language is a body of evidence, that Bedouin speech is the evidence, and that a rule the evidence does not bear is not a rule. The student takes it further than the master, into a system the master never attempted.
suggested_refs: Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', canonical Qur'an reader and Basran grammarian

stops.name: Basra, the Ibadi inheritance
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: English Wikipedia calls him a companion of Jabir ibn Zayd, who died around 93 AH, some twenty-five years before al-Khalil's birth, so no personal association is possible; the claim survives only as one about milieu
stops.campa: Oman is Ibadi ground and his people are Omani, so the tradition puts him young in the circles of Jabir ibn Zayd, whom the Ibadis count among their founding figures and who took the leadership after Abd Allah ibn Ibad. The arithmetic forbids the meeting: Jabir is dead before al-Khalil is born. What remains once the meeting is removed is the milieu, a household and a tribe formed by that school. The biographers do not notice the gap, and the gap does not close.
suggested_refs: Jabir ibn Zayd and the formation of Ibadism in Basra and Oman

stops.name: Basra, the circle of 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Arabic teacher lists; undated
stops.campa: 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi teaches grammar in the same city and the Arabic lists put him among al-Khalil's masters. Between these men the Basran school assembles the apparatus Sibawayh will one day write down: that speech has an underlying form and surface forms derived from it, that an irregularity is a rule working under pressure. None of them leaves a book that survives. Their work reaches later centuries because their student's student wrote it out and named them on nearly every page.
suggested_refs: 'Isa ibn 'Umar al-Thaqafi and the early Basran grammatical school
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي', teacher list

stops.name: Basra, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani turns him
stops.date_confidence: attested by Britannica and English Wikipedia; undated, and how far the shift is documented rather than deduced from his tribal background is disputed
stops.campa: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, traditionist of Basra, argues him out of the Ibadi doctrine of his upbringing and into the Sunni majority. Nothing in the later work is sectarian; the meters and the dictionary belong to no party and are used by everyone within a century. He changes schools on an argument and goes back to the same ring in the same mosque. No source records a quarrel over it, and no line of the doctrine he left shows up in anything he wrote afterwards.
suggested_refs: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Basran traditionist, named in the conversion account

stops.name: Al-Mirbad, the market where the language is collected
stops.date_confidence: al-Mirbad's role is standard background for Basran philology; al-Khalil's personal presence there is not individually documented and the pin is approximate
stops.campa: On the edge of the city, where the caravans come in, al-Mirbad is a camel market that doubles as a court of the Arabic language. Bedouin arrive carrying the speech the grammarians treat as the standard; poets recite for money and for reputation; philologists stand at the edge writing down a rare plural or a verb no townsman uses. This is the fieldwork that fills the Basran books. That al-Khalil worked in this way is plain from what his own books contain.
suggested_refs: Al-Mirbad, camel market and literary gathering ground on the outskirts of Old Basra
sources: General histories of Basran grammar on al-Mirbad as the philologists' meeting ground

segments.name: The Anvil and the Five Circles

stops.name: Basra, the reed hut
stops.date_confidence: attested for his adult life in Basra; the sources describe the house and its income without dating either
stops.campa: He lives in a hut of reeds among the reed huts of Basra, keeping himself on a garden he inherited and on birds he flies for game. Governors offer him money and he does not take it. His students go out from this doorway into salaries and reputations while he cannot lay hands on two coins, and the report comes from one of them, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, with no embarrassment in it. He is living this way already when the meters are worked out, and living this way still when the dictionary is being dictated to a student on the floor.
stops.quote: أقام الخليل في خصّ (كوخ) من أخصاص البصرة، لا يقدر على فلسين
stops.quote_source: Attributed to his student al-Nadr ibn Shumayl; Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي', following the Ibn Khallikan tradition
suggested_refs: The reed-built quarters of Old Basra described in the tabaqat accounts of al-Khalil's household

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba and the yearly pilgrimage
stops.date_confidence: attested that he performed the pilgrimage annually; no individual year is recorded and this date stands for all of them
stops.campa: Every year, the biographers say, he goes down the pilgrim road from Basra to the Hijaz and circles the House. It is the only travel his life contains. A man who will not take a governor's purse pays for the journey out of a garden's income and walks home the same way, and the piety is reported in the same breath as the poverty, as one fact and not two. On one of these returns, in the version most often told, he hears the sound that will give Arabic poetry its measure.
stops.quote_source: al-Marzubani on al-Khalil; Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي'
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and al-Masjid al-Haram, station of his annual pilgrimage

stops.name: Medina, the Prophet's Mosque on the pilgrim road
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source documents al-Khalil at Medina. The stop follows the ordinary hajj practice of a Basran pilgrim in this period and nothing more
stops.campa: The road from Basra to Mecca commonly turns aside at Medina, where the Prophet lies beneath his mosque and pilgrims pray the length of their stay. No biographer puts al-Khalil in that courtyard, and the road he took is reconstructed from what pilgrims of his century ordinarily did. What the sources keep of these journeys is the going out and the coming back: a man leaves a reed hut once a year, circles the House, and returns to the reed hut. One of those returns carries the anvil home with it.
suggested_refs: Al-Masjid an-Nabawi at Medina, customary station of the Basra to Mecca pilgrim route
sources: Inference from standard hajj-route practice; not attested for al-Khalil in any source consulted

stops.name: Basra, the hammers of the Suq al-Saffarin
stops.date_confidence: traditional anecdote surviving in two incompatible versions: the Arabic tradition gives the coppersmiths' market, English Wikipedia a single blacksmith's anvil heard on the way back from pilgrimage. Neither fixes a date and no source locates the market
stops.campa: The coppersmiths of Basra beat sheet metal in a street of their own, and the beating is not random: it falls into figures, long and short, repeated and varied. He is walking through it, or he is coming home from Mecca and hears one anvil, depending on which book tells it. What he hears is that the sound has feet. Out of hammering he takes a notation for the thing Arabic poets had been doing correctly for two centuries without any of them being able to say what it was.
suggested_refs: Suq al-Saffarin, the coppersmiths' market of Basra, named in the Arabic version of the anecdote

stops.name: Basra, the fifteen meters and the five circles
stops.date_confidence: attested that he described fifteen meters and laid them out on five circles; the treatise al-'Arud is not extant and is known through later citation, and no date can be given for its composition
stops.campa: He writes out the whole prosody of Arabic as fifteen meters and arranges them on five circles, each circle a family in which one meter becomes its neighbour by a shift in where the line is cut. It is not a list. It is a device that generates the list and shows why there are no others. The book, al-'Arud, does not survive. The system does, entire, because every poet and every critic after him works inside it and needs no copy of the book to do so.
suggested_refs: The five circles of al-Khalil, reconstructed from citation in later works on 'ilm al-'arud

stops.name: Basra, three meters no pre-Islamic poet used
stops.date_confidence: the statement that three meters were unknown to pre-Islamic Arabia is attested flatly and names none of them; that he invented them is an inference drawn from that fact and is not settled
stops.campa: Of the fifteen, three are found in no poetry from before Islam. The circles predict them; the corpus does not contain them. Either the old poets used them and nothing survived, or the system produced patterns nobody had yet composed in and he wrote them into the language. The second reading makes the grammarian an inventor of forms, which is a larger thing than the descriptive science he is credited with founding. The sources give the number three and name none of the three.
suggested_refs: The three meters unattested in pre-Islamic verse, discussed in the scholarly literature on al-'arud

stops.name: Basra, the dots give way to shapes
stops.date_confidence: attested as his innovation; the sources describe the replacement of the earlier dot notation without giving any chronology for it
stops.campa: Before him a short vowel is a dot, and dots already carry too much work in a script that uses them to tell one consonant from another. He replaces the dots with shapes: small letters riding above and below the line, an alif laid down for one vowel, a waw curled for the second, a ya set beneath for the third. Being miniature letters, they can be read at speed and never confused with the skeleton under them. He devises them for poetry. They end on the Qur'an.
suggested_refs: The harakat system of vowel marks, replacing the coloured-dot notation of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali

stops.name: Basra, the small shin above the doubled letter
stops.date_confidence: attested; undated
stops.campa: For a consonant pronounced twice he sets a small shin above it, the head of the word shadda, and a doubling that had lived only in the reciter's memory becomes visible on the page. The whole apparatus works this way: each mark is an abbreviation of the Arabic word for what the mark does. A system built out of the language's own names for its own sounds can be taught in an afternoon, and it is still taught that way, unchanged in principle, in the schools that use the script.
suggested_refs: The shadda as a reduced shin, in the standard account of Arabic diacritical development

stops.name: Basra, the plan of a book that holds every word
stops.date_confidence: attested that he conceived and began the work; the date is inferred only from his having left it unfinished at his death
stops.campa: Nobody has yet made a dictionary of Arabic. He decides to make one that is complete, not a gathering of hard words but the whole lexicon, and to prove the completeness by construction: take the roots of two, three, four and five letters, permute the letters of each, and walk the permutations marking which are words and which the language has left empty. It is a combinatorial argument made before there is a name for one. The book is called Kitab al-'Ayn.
suggested_refs: Kitab al-'Ayn, the first dictionary of Arabic and the oldest to survive

stops.name: Basra, beginning at the throat
stops.date_confidence: attested arrangement; the twenty-six-book structure is described in the standard accounts, undated
stops.campa: He does not order the entries by the alphabet. He orders them by the mouth, starting at the deepest point of articulation and moving outward: 'ayn first, out of the throat, and mim last, at the lips. To find a word you must know where in your own head you make its first sound. The scheme is a phonetician's scheme, which is what he is, and the letter he begins from gives the book its name, because 'ayn comes up from the floor of the throat and so stands for itself.
stops.quote: It is said that al-Farahidi's Kitab al-'Ayn did for lexicography what his student Sibawayh's al-Kitab did for grammar.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Kitab al-Ayn', given there as a hedged scholarly comparison
suggested_refs: The articulatory ordering of Kitab al-'Ayn, from pharyngeal 'ayn to labial mim

stops.name: Basra, dictating to al-Layth ibn al-Muzaffar
stops.date_confidence: attested in the Arabic account that he conceived the work and directed al-Layth to write it; the division of labour between master and student is debated by specialists and unresolved
stops.campa: The work is dictated. Al-Layth ibn al-Muzaffar ibn Nasr, his student, takes it down and will finish what is unfinished when the master is dead. How much of the surviving text is al-Khalil's and how much al-Layth's has been argued for a thousand years without a settlement, and some hold the whole redaction is the student's. He dictates here as he dictates everywhere. The prosody and the cipher book went out of the world the same way, and what is left of either sits inside books signed by other men.
suggested_refs: Al-Layth ibn al-Muzaffar ibn Nasr, redactor and completer of Kitab al-'Ayn

segments.name: The Circle of the Reed Hut

stops.name: Basra, al-Asma'i in the circle
stops.date_confidence: attested student list; undated
stops.campa: Al-Asma'i comes to him and will become the great collector of Bedouin verse, the man later centuries quote whenever they want to know what an old poet actually said. From the master he takes the habit of treating desert speech as evidence to be gathered and checked rather than admired. The circle in the reed hut is producing, inside a single generation, the philologists on whose collections the whole Arabic literary canon will rest, and their teacher cannot afford two coins.
suggested_refs: Al-Asma'i, philologist and transmitter of Bedouin poetry, trained in al-Khalil's circle
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'al-Khalil ibn Ahmad', student list

stops.name: Basra, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and the road east
stops.date_confidence: attested student list; undated
stops.campa: Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl sits in the same circle and will carry Basran philology east into Khurasan, where a school forms around him. He is also the witness who reports his teacher's poverty, and the report is not pity but the boast of a student who watched a man refuse what was put in front of him. The method travels with him. Within two generations there are grammarians in the Persian east arguing Basran cases, and the dictionary itself will one day come back west out of that country.
suggested_refs: Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, who carried Basran philology into Khurasan
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'al-Khalil ibn Ahmad', student list

stops.name: Basra, a Persian arrives from Shiraz
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the window: Sibawayh was born about 760 and al-Khalil died in 786, so the study falls roughly between 775 and 786. Any account placing it under Harun al-Rashid is impossible, as his reign begins in 786
stops.campa: Sibawayh, born near Shiraz, comes to Basra as a young man for hadith and stays for grammar. The sources say he was more indebted to al-Khalil than to any other teacher, and the debt is measurable, which is rare in this century. He will write one book. It is called simply al-Kitab, the Book, and it fixes the description of Arabic so completely that no later grammarian works outside it. Everything in it that begins 'he said' with no name attached means the man in the reed hut.
suggested_refs: Al-Kitab of Sibawayh, foundational grammar of Arabic, composed after study under al-Khalil

stops.name: Basra, the governor's offer refused
stops.date_confidence: recurrent anecdote in the biographical tradition; the governor is not named, the wording varies between tellings, and no year is given
stops.campa: A governor offers him a stipend, or offers and then withholds it, and he answers with a sentence that is not about money: the one who gave him a mouth undertook to feed it, and a refusal enriches nobody. He sends verse after it, telling Sulayman he is at ease without him and rich though he owns nothing. Then he goes back to the hut. The anecdote is told in a dozen forms because every teller wanted it, and the man it describes behaves the same way in all of them.
stops.quote: He, who formed me with a mouth, engaged to give me nourishment till such a time as He takes me to Himself. Thou hast refused me a trifling sum, but that refusal will not increase thy wealth.
stops.quote_source: Attributed reply to a governor; English Wikipedia, 'Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi', following the Ibn Khallikan tradition (Wafayat al-A'yan, trans. de Slane)
suggested_refs: The verse to Sulayman refusing patronage, preserved in the Arabic biographical tradition

stops.name: Basra, six hundred and eight times
stops.date_confidence: attested count from the standard summary of al-Kitab; al-Kitab itself cannot be dated more closely than Sibawayh's short life, c. 760-796
stops.campa: In al-Kitab, Sibawayh quotes his teacher six hundred and eight times, more than any other authority in the book. He has no shelf of his own. His name comes back instead through a student's pages, in the third person, answering questions put to him on paper years after the sessions ended. The treatise on meters and the book of ciphers reach later centuries by the same route, quoted inside books that were copied when theirs were not. He does not appear to have minded.
suggested_refs: The 608 citations of al-Khalil in Sibawayh's al-Kitab

stops.name: Basra, the four kinds of people
stops.date_confidence: attested sayings, undated; the fourfold saying circulates widely in later collections and could not be traced to a single named classical work
stops.campa: He sorts people by what they know and by whether they know that they know it, and tells his students to take knowledge from the first sort and to teach the one who is merely unaware. He holds that a man's reason stands at its full at forty. What his contemporaries remember above the sayings is the quality of his attention: when his door was shut, his mind did not go past it, and the students outside learned to wait until it opened rather than knock on it. The sayings pass from collection to collection for a thousand years without an author's name attached to any of them but his.
stops.quote: الناس أربعة: فرجلٌ يدري وهو يدري أنه يدري، فذاك عالمٌ فخذوا عنه
stops.quote_source: Attributed to al-Khalil; Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي' (opening of the fourfold saying)
suggested_refs: The fourfold saying on knowledge attributed to al-Khalil in the later gnomic collections

stops.name: Basra, wealthy with no money
stops.date_confidence: attested as a summary of his reported views; the phrasing belongs to the encyclopedic source and rests on unspecified classical citation
stops.campa: He holds that poverty is not the absence of coin but a condition of the soul, and that by that measure he is a rich man. He quotes a line of al-Akhtal at his students to the effect that no treasure is the equal of good conduct. The doctrine suits a man who has chosen to own nothing, and it is also the reason he can go on choosing it for forty years while the students he trained take posts and salaries and come back to sit on the floor of his hut and be taught for nothing.
stops.quote: If thou wantest treasures, thou wilt find none equal to a virtuous conduct.
stops.quote_source: A line of al-Akhtal quoted by al-Farahidi; English Wikipedia, 'Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi'
suggested_refs: The Views section of the biographical tradition on al-Khalil's understanding of poverty

stops.name: Basra, Kitab al-Mu'amma
stops.date_confidence: attested by the modern histories of cryptography as written before 786; the treatise is not extant and is known only through later citation
stops.campa: The same combinatorics that built the dictionary he turns on secret writing. Kitab al-Mu'amma sets out how to enumerate every possible Arabic word, with vowels and without, by permutation, and so how to attack a message written in a script that hides them. Historians of cryptology call it the first work of its kind by a linguist. The book is lost. What survives is the description of its method in later hands, and the fact that the next man to write on ciphers in Arabic starts from it.
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Mu'amma, the Book of Cryptographic Messages, known through citation

stops.name: Baghdad, a cryptogram he could not have read
stops.date_confidence: chronologically impossible as told: al-Ma'mun's reign begins in 813, at least twenty-seven years after al-Khalil's death, and no encyclopedic or cryptology-history source consulted attaches this episode to his name at all
stops.campa: A story runs through the popular histories: a Byzantine cipher arrives at the court of the caliph al-Ma'mun, nobody at the court can open it, and al-Khalil breaks it by permutation. The dates forbid it. Al-Ma'mun rules from 813 and al-Khalil has been dead since 786 or thereabouts, and neither the Arabic nor the English encyclopedias put the episode under his name. The story survives because it wants a man who reasons his way into a locked language, and that man existed.
suggested_refs: Mrayati, Alam and al-Tayyan, 'Arabic Origins of Cryptology', for the primary sourcing this legend still lacks

stops.name: Baghdad, al-Kindi builds on him
stops.date_confidence: attested that al-Kindi built on al-Khalil's work; al-Kindi's own dates are about 801 to 873 and the treatise is undated within them
stops.campa: Two generations later al-Kindi, serving al-Ma'mun and al-Mu'tasim in Baghdad, writes the Risala fi Istikhraj al-Kutub al-Mu'amma and introduces frequency analysis, the counting of letters that turns codebreaking into a science. The reference works say plainly that he is building on al-Khalil. What al-Kindi adds is statistics; what he inherits is the conviction that a language is a finite structure whose possibilities can be laid out and searched to the end.
stops.quote: Building on the work of al-Khalil (717-786), Al-Kindi's book entitled Manuscript on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages...
suggested_refs: Risala fi Istikhraj al-Kutub al-Mu'amma of al-Kindi, the first treatise on frequency analysis

stops.name: Basra, an arithmetic for the maidservant
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the accounting-and-maidservant motive is a narrative elaboration transmitted in the biographical dictionaries, not an attested event
stops.campa: His servant is being cheated by the greengrocer, and he sets out to build her a system of reckoning simple enough that she cannot be cheated again. It is the last problem he is known to have worked on: not a meter, not a root, but a method of counting for a woman who buys vegetables. He gives a household ledger the attention he gave the meters of the Arabs. He is still inside the problem when he gets up, opens the door and walks out into the street.
suggested_refs: The greengrocer anecdote in the Death section of the biographical tradition

stops.name: Basra, the pillar in the mosque
stops.date_confidence: the death in Basra is secure; the pillar is transmitted by al-Dhahabi in the fourteenth century about an eighth-century death, and the year is disputed between 170 AH (786/7), 173 AH (789/90) and 174 AH (790/1)
stops.campa: Working the problem in his head, he walks into the mosque and into one of its pillars, and the injury kills him. Al-Dhahabi transmits the pillar centuries afterwards; the English books add the greengrocer. That he died in Basra is as firm as anything in the life. The year is not: the traditions give 170, 173 and 174 of the Hijra, and the conversions in circulation have been mismatched so often that the disagreement between the Arabic and European accounts looks wider than it is.
stops.quote: While he was deeply absorbed in contemplation of a system of accounting to save his maidservant from being cheated by the green grocer, he wandered into a mosque, and there he absent-mindedly bumped into a pillar and was fatally injured.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi', Death section
suggested_refs: Al-Dhahabi's notice of al-Khalil's death, the earliest named transmitter of the pillar account
sources: Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي', citing al-Dhahabi

stops.name: Basra, a grave no source names
stops.date_confidence: burial in Basra is general consensus across the Arabic and European accounts; no consulted source names a tomb, a quarter or a surviving gravesite
stops.campa: He is buried in the city he left only to pray at Mecca. No source consulted names the place. There is no dome over him, no visiting day, no shrine: the man who gave Arabic its meters and its vowel marks has no grave anyone can point to, and the city that will one day set his statue at the head of a street cannot say where he lies. What he left in place of a monument is a book unfinished on a table, a system of marks, a set of circles, and a room of students who knew exactly what to do with all of it.
stops.quote: من أحب أن ينظر إلى رجلٍ خلق من الذهب والمسك فلينظر إلى الخليل بن أحمد
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna; Arabic Wikipedia, 'الخليل بن أحمد الفراهيدي'
suggested_refs: The absence of any recorded tomb of al-Khalil in Basra, noted as a gap in the sources

stops.name: Basra, al-Layth finishes the 'Ayn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the completion by al-Layth and other students is attested in outline, the division of labour disputed, and no date is given for the finished redaction
stops.campa: Al-Layth ibn al-Muzaffar takes up the dictionary where it stopped and carries it to an end, with other students in some accounts. The text that circulates afterwards is theirs as much as his, and the scholars who later doubt whether al-Khalil wrote any of it are still arguing about a book he certainly designed. Twenty-six books in one work, ordered by the throat and the palate and the lips, complete by construction: no redactor arrives at that plan by accident.
suggested_refs: The transmission history of Kitab al-'Ayn from al-Khalil's dictation to al-Layth's redaction

stops.name: Nishapur, the manuscript in the Tahirid library
stops.date_confidence: reported transmission with no chain of custody given; the Tahirid holding is traditional and the date is a loose inference from the 862 sale
stops.campa: The original is reported to pass east into the library of the Tahirid governors of Khurasan, the province al-Nadr ibn Shumayl had carried Basran grammar into. A book made out of the speech of Iraqi Bedouin sits in a Persian city, kept by a dynasty ruling for the caliphs, until a bookseller decides it is worth more where it came from. The route out and the route back are the same road the philology took, east with the students and west again as merchandise.
suggested_refs: The Tahirid library of Khurasan in the transmission account of Kitab al-'Ayn

stops.name: Basra, fifty dinars for the book that was made here
stops.date_confidence: attested to 862 or 863 CE in the standard account of the manuscript's return, about seventy years after his death
stops.campa: About seventy years after his death a bookseller from northeastern Persia brings the manuscript to Basra and sells it for fifty dinars. The city buys back its own dictionary. Nobody in the transaction is in a position to check the text against a man who dictated it from memory in a reed hut and left it unfinished, and from this point every copy descends from a copy. The price is recorded because the sale was remarkable. The seller's name is not recorded at all.
suggested_refs: The 862/863 sale of the Kitab al-'Ayn manuscript at Basra for fifty dinars

stops.name: Cordoba, the 'Ayn in al-Andalus
stops.date_confidence: reported circulation in al-Andalus around 914 or 915, transmitted without a chain; al-Zubaydi's abridgement is dated only by his death in 989
stops.campa: Within two centuries the book, or material taken out of it, is in Islamic Spain, four thousand miles from the market where the hammers rang. Abu Bakr al-Zubaydi of Cordoba will cut it down to a summary before he dies in 989. In the same century the method itself crosses into another language: Saadia Gaon compiles the Agron, the first Hebrew lexicon, saying openly that he is doing for Hebrew what the grammarians of Basra and Kufa did for Arabic. The founder of that Basran school has been dead a hundred and fifty years.
suggested_refs: Abu Bakr al-Zubaydi's abridgement of Kitab al-'Ayn, made in al-Andalus before 989

stops.name: Baghdad, Ibn al-Nadim writes him into the Fihrist
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fihrist is begun in 987 and the work continues into 988. Ibn al-Nadim was Baghdad-born and Baghdad-based, and travelled to Basra, Kufa, Aleppo and Mosul hunting material
stops.campa: A Baghdad bookseller's son sets out to list every book written in Arabic. Ibn al-Nadim, who travels to Basra and Kufa and Aleppo hunting titles but works out of his family's shop, enters al-Khalil with his works: prosody, phonetics, the rest. Because he does it, a man two centuries dead has a bibliography, and later readers can tell by name what has been lost. Most of what is known of the shape of al-Khalil's output survives because a cataloguer would not leave anything out.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Nadim's al-Fihrist, compiled at Baghdad from 987, listing al-Khalil's works

stops.name: Baghdad, the announcement in Lughat al-Arab
stops.date_confidence: attested that the discovery of the lost text was announced in 1914 in the Baghdad journal Lughat al-Arab; who found the manuscript, and which manuscript it was, is not stated in any source consulted
stops.campa: In 1914 the Baghdad journal Lughat al-Arab announces that the lost text of the first Arabic dictionary has been found. The journal is edited by Anastase-Marie al-Karmali, a Carmelite of Baghdad, and he is the publicist and not the finder; who found it, and which manuscript it was, the sources do not say. The book goes back into print in the twentieth century in eight volumes, and in 2003 in four volumes rearranged alphabetically, which undoes the one thing about it that was new.
suggested_refs: Lughat al-Arab (Baghdad), 1914, announcing the recovery of Kitab al-'Ayn

stops.name: Basra, the statue at the head of Independence Street
stops.date_confidence: attested: English Wikipedia gives 1965 to 1970 for the sculpture, the Arabic entry places it on Sharia al-Istiqlal without a date. The pin is modern Basra, some fifteen kilometres from the old city he lived in
stops.campa: Modern Basra stands on the Shatt al-Arab, some fifteen kilometres from the mound where the old city was, the whole town having been moved a century after his death. It puts him in bronze at the entrance to Sharia al-Istiqlal. The man had no grave that anyone recorded; he gets a statue instead, in a city that walked away from the one he lived in, in a country that had by then spent a thousand years writing its poetry in his meters and pointing its Qur'ans with his marks.
suggested_refs: The statue of al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi at the entrance to Independence Street, Basra

stops.name: Rustaq, a primary school with his name on it
stops.date_confidence: modern and undated in the source; the date stands only as a marker for present-day commemoration
stops.campa: In Oman, at Rustaq under the mountains, children learn to read in a building called the Al Khalil Bin Ahmed Al Farahidi School of Basic Education. Whether he was born in this country or only descended from people who left it, the books still disagree. Oman has settled the question in its own favour by putting his name over the doorway, above pupils sounding out the vowel marks he cut into the script and scanning lines in meters he set on a circle. The evidence has not moved in twelve centuries. The daily use has.
suggested_refs: Al Khalil Bin Ahmed Al Farahidi School of Basic Education, Rustaq, Oman

stops.name: Birkat al-Mouz, the centre at the University of Nizwa
stops.date_confidence: single-sourced and undated: the centre is asserted only in the article on al-Khalil and is not confirmed in the university's own encyclopedic entry, which lists no research centres
stops.campa: Twenty kilometres northwest of Nizwa, at the foot of the Green Mountain, the University of Nizwa is reported to run a centre carrying his name. The university's own entry names no research centres at all, so a single line elsewhere is carrying the whole claim. Whatever the centre turns out to be, the claim behind it is plain: Ibadi Oman takes for its own the grammarian who was argued out of Ibadism, on the strength of a tribe and a nisba that means young lion.
suggested_refs: The Al Khalil bin Ahmed Al Farahidi Center, University of Nizwa, Birkat al-Mouz, Oman
